extracted.intended_audience: writers and essayists (readers interested in prose style, conversation, and social satire)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for composing essays, descriptive pieces (e.g., gardens, fashions), epistolary sketches, and satirical conversation — focusing on order, vivid particulars, voice, and rhetorical devices. Grounded in 18th‑century Spectator essays but applicable to general prose craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodical structure vs. irregular genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Method is of advantage to a Work ... Irregularity and want of Method are only supportable in Men of great Learning or Genius, who are often too full to be exact, and therefore chuse to throw down their Pearls in Heaps before the Reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodical discourse should be planned so thoughts follow one another in a regular series: it helps invention, makes each thought more intelligible, discovers the drift and meaning, and lets every part show in its greatest beauty. Irregular, rambling arrangements are permissible only for writers of very high learning/genius whose abundance of idea supplies value despite lack of order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use method to aid both writer and reader
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Man has plann'd his Discourse, he finds a great many Thoughts rising out of every Head ... His Thoughts are ... better discover their Drift and Meaning, when they are placed in their proper Lights, and follow one another in a regular Series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the scheme before writing: outlining heads reveals more supporting ideas and allows clearer exposition; readers comprehend, take pleasure, and retain material better from methodical arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method required in ordinary conversation to be understood
rubrics_metrics.description: Method is not less requisite in ordinary Conversation than in Writing, provided a Man would talk to make himself understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid aimless disputation; keep the point and logical sequence in spoken debates. Example: coffee-house arguments that lose the question after three sentences are failures of method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'a barren Superfluity of Words' — prune rambling discursiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Man who does not know how to methodize his Thoughts, has always, to borrow a Phrase from the Dispensary, 'a barren Superfluity of Words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent diffuse, showy loquacity (the Tom Puzzle type) by demanding what the speaker is trying to prove; favor concise, purposeful expression (the Mr. Dry model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular/rambling composition as a descriptive mode (wood vs. plantation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When I read an Author of Genius who writes without Method, I fancy myself in a Wood that abounds with a great many noble Objects, rising among one another in the greatest Confusion and Disorder. When I read a methodical Discourse, I am in a regular Plantation ... Your Eye commands the whole Prospect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rambling, associative structures when the goal is exploratory, discovery-driven prose (evocative, many surprises); use methodical order when you want the reader to grasp an overall plan or argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange descriptive particulars to create compositional effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The only Method I observe in this Particular, is to range in the same Quarter the Products of the same Season, that they may make their Appearance together, and compose a Picture of the greatest Variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group related sensory/details (seasonal plants, colors, sounds) spatially or thematically to form coherent 'pictures' and maximize variety and effect in description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural, wild variety over forced artifice in landscape/garden description
rubrics_metrics.description: My Compositions in Gardening are altogether after the Pindarick Manner, and run into the beautiful Wildness of Nature, without affecting the nicer Elegancies of Art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for the pleasures of the imagination, emphasize spontaneity, profusion, and native growth rather than over-stylized or artificial ornament; celebrate informal contrasts (kitchen produce vs. orangery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrasts and engineered views for dramatic description
rubrics_metrics.description: To give this particular Spot of Ground the greater Effect, they have made a very pleasing Contrast; for as on one side of the Walk you see this hollow Basin ... on the other side of it there appears a seeming Mount ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy spatial contrasts (hollow vs. mount, cultivated vs. wild) to surprise the reader and heighten aesthetic appreciation; explain how features juxtapose to form an intentional scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ concrete sensory details and living elements to enliven prose
rubrics_metrics.description: My Pockets stuffed with Bread to dispense my Favours ... a Fountain rising ... Banks of Violets and Primroses ... the glowing Redness of the Berries ... I value my Garden more for being full of Blackbirds than Cherries ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate descriptions with tactile, visual, auditory particulars (bread for dogs, birdsong, colors, fountains) to make scenes immediate and pleasurable to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial foreign-name dropping in travel/observational writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The most irksome Conversation ... among Travellers, who have passed through France and Italy ... Their distinguishing Mark is certain Prettinesses of Foreign Languages, the Meaning of which they could have better express'd in their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't substitute lists of place-names, church fineries, or foreign phrases for genuine observation and interpretation; prefer conveying meaning and experience over mere name-dropping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical exaggeration and mock-institution as rhetorical device
rubrics_metrics.description: There should certainly therefore in each County be established a Club of the Persons whose Conversations I have described ... Their Attire should be the same with their Huntsmen's, and none should be admitted ... except he had broke his Collar-bone thrice ... The President must necessarily have broken his Neck ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overstated premises (clubs for the maimed, repositories for fashions) and ludicrous qualifications to expose social follies; construct absurd institutional details (mottos, architecture, appointment rules) for comic critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture authentic voice and naiveté in epistolary or character sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: Letter: 'Mr. Shapely is the prettiest Gentleman about Town. He is very tall, but not too tall neither. He dances like a Angel. His Mouth is made I don't know how ...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproduce the speaker's level of knowledge, repetition, concrete obsessions (appearance, dancing, Latin), and naïve reasoning to render convincing characterful letters or first‑person sketches; small, idiosyncratic details signal youth and sincerity.
